name: Aisha Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is kept confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day is like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I patrol the east side, around Station Road and the Hillcrest estates, which is where I grew up. A day shift starts with briefing at seven, then it's calls: a stolen moped, a shop owner with a man who won't leave, an elderly lady who's fallen and can't reach the phone. Half the time someone recognises me from school or from the mosque. I like that; people talk to someone they know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being useful in a place I care about. The hard part is the nights, and the days when you see the same young lads going the same wrong way. I don't use AI, I never have. My fiancé Yusuf works in a bank's mortgage office, and he says they use it all the time, but I'd rather do things myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people get on with real work. I don't post much, but at the dinner table I'd say I always thought it was overblown. Police work is people, and you can't hand people to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My job stays, Yusuf's job stays, and we can carry on with the wedding next summer as planned. Our real worry is money for the wedding and for a flat, because prices round here keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I'd keep putting 300 a month aside for the wedding and our first flat, which is about four months of my pay saved up now. If the force brings in some small AI thing, I'd do the training and then go back to writing my own reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding next summer. How much does that weigh on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot. My mother wants three hundred guests and I want about half that. We'll meet in the middle, but the middle is still expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone at the station who's excited about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let them be excited. I'd just say a computer never sat with an old woman on her kitchen floor waiting for an ambulance. Someone has to do that, and it should be a person.

say: I'd say good, let people get on with **real work**.
At home I'd say it was always **overblown**.
think: I'm **relieved**: my job and Yusuf's job both stay.
Our real worry is paying for the **wedding** and a first flat.
do: Keep saving **300 a month** for the wedding and a flat.
Do any AI training required, then **write my own reports**.
S0.quote: A computer never sat with an old woman on her kitchen floor waiting for an ambulance.
fieldNote: She patrols **where she grew up** and draws meaning from being known.
Her real pressure is **wedding costs** and family expectations.
She politely **refuses AI** for herself without judging colleagues.

steps.text: Keep patrolling Station Road and the Hillcrest estates
Keep saving 300 a month for the wedding and a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say jobs come and go, and people have to work hard and learn something new. I wouldn't moan about it. I'd say the government should pay for apprenticeships, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Yusuf I'd worry about. Checking mortgage forms is exactly what you're describing, so his office would shrink first. My job is mostly on my feet, so it'd be the reports that change, but his could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Yusuf about a smaller wedding, maybe at the community hall instead of a venue, and save the difference. We'd keep both our savings in one place. And I'd ask my uncle, who has a car repair garage, whether Yusuf could learn something there if his office cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, anxious for him. I'd pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Yusuf take the suggestion about your uncle's garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well at first. My fiancé Yusuf did three years of college to get that desk job, and Yusuf's mother is very proud of it. But he's practical, and he'd come round if his office started cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut the wedding. What would your mother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset for a week. Then she'd tell everyone it was her idea to be sensible. That's how my mother works.

say: I'd say people must **work hard** and learn something new.
I'd say the government should pay for **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: **Yusuf's office** checks mortgage forms, so it would shrink first.
My job is **on my feet**, so mostly the reports would change.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding** at the community hall and save the difference.
Ask my uncle about **garage work** for Yusuf if his office cuts staff.
S1.quote: My fiancé Yusuf did three years of college to get that desk job, and Yusuf's mother is very proud of it.
fieldNote: Her worry centres on her **fiancé's desk job**, not her own.
She prefers **family networks** and apprenticeships to state support.
The **wedding size** is where money pressure shows first.

steps.text: Move the wedding to the community hall and cut the guest list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless. Big companies would be making the money and ordinary families would pay for AGI. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep people in real jobs, and I'd tell my family to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Yusuf's job goes in 2028, nearly straight away. Mine would lose the reports and paperwork at the same time, and then by 2031 the robots could do the patrol too. That means both of us, in our early thirties, with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married sooner and much smaller, just a nikah at the mosque and dinner at my parents' house, and keep the money. We'd live with my parents for a couple of years instead of renting. I'd stop every extra, the gym, the takeaways, the new phone. And I'd lean on family, because that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the ground's going from under both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Living with your parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crowded. My two younger brothers are still at home and the flat has three bedrooms. But my father would say a family that sticks together gets through anything, and he'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'no plan'. What would you need to make one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mainly, and someone to tell me straight what jobs would still exist. I don't use these tools, so I wouldn't even know where to start looking. That's the honest truth.

say: I'd say this is **reckless**, with big firms profiting and families paying.
I'd **vote** for whoever keeps people in real jobs.
think: **Yusuf's job** goes in 2028, nearly straight away.
By **2031** robots could do my patrol, leaving us both with no plan.
do: Marry sooner with just a **nikah** and family dinner.
Live with **my parents** for two years instead of renting.
Cut the **gym, takeaways** and new phone.
feel: **Scared**, as if the ground is going from under them both.
S2.quote: Big companies would be making the money and ordinary families would pay for AGI.
fieldNote: Both household incomes look **at risk**, his first and hers later.
Her answer is **family**: marry small, move in with parents.
Admits she has **no plan** and wouldn't know where to start.

steps.text: Marry sooner with a nikah at the mosque instead of a big wedding
Cancel the gym, takeaways and the new phone
Move in with her parents for two years instead of renting
Vote for candidates who promise to keep people in real jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, that families shouldn't pay for big firms' profits. But with five years I'd add that people should use the time to learn a trade. I'd say it to the young lads I stop on the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still hard. Yusuf's office would start shrinking well before 2031, so he'd have a few years to move. I'd be 32 when the paperwork goes and 35 when the robots come. That's young enough to change, but I don't know what to change to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding next summer, but at the community hall. Yusuf would start an evening course in electrical work in the first year, because hands-on trades have the extra three years. I'd save harder, 400 a month instead of 300. I'd stay put and keep policing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened than the fast one, but it doesn't leave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push Yusuf to retrain but not yourself. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his job goes first, and mine is still useful for a while. And honestly, because I'm stubborn about my job. I chose it, I'm good at it, and I'm not ready to let it go for a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young lads on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads on the Hillcrest estate to get an apprenticeship with a plumber or an electrician while those still exist. I'd say it on the street, not on social media.

I'd tell people to use the time to **learn a trade**.
think: Yusuf's office shrinks before 2031, so he has **a few years** to move.
At **32 and 35** I could change, but I don't know to what.
do: Keep the wedding next summer at the **community hall**.
Push Yusuf onto an evening **electrical course** in year one.
feel: **Anxious**; less frightened than the fast version, but it stays with her.
S3.quote: I'd tell the lads on the Hillcrest estate to get an apprenticeship with a plumber or an electrician while those still exist.
fieldNote: She pushes her **fiancé to retrain** but holds on to her own job.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer at the community hall
Raise savings from 300 to 400 a month
Keep patrolling the east side and turn down any move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for people to sort themselves out if they work for it. I wouldn't want the government stepping in with handouts. I'd say schools should start teaching trades again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough breathing room. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and nearly 40 when robots come. Yusuf would have time to move into something else, and we'd have children by then, God willing, so I'd be thinking about them more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, we'd have the wedding next summer as planned, maybe a bit smaller. We'd keep saving 300 a month and look at buying a small flat near my parents in the next two years. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff unless the force made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have children by then. Does that change how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. If my kids are small when the robots come, I want to be home more, not less. Maybe that's when I'd leave policing, and Yusuf earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this one worse than it sounds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people waste the ten years, like they always do. Everyone says there's time, and then there isn't. My father says that about his pension.

I'd say **schools** should start teaching trades again, not handouts.
think: Ten years feels like **breathing room** for both of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Yusuf and I would both be hit and there'd be no time. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, paid, so people can learn a trade without going broke. Not handouts, but a real way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things fall apart, people round here go to the mosque, the church, their families. I don't think a machine can replace that, and I hope nobody tries.

headlineQuote: When things fall apart, people round here go to the mosque, the church, their families.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old patrol officer** on the east side, where she grew up, and never uses AI.
She is **engaged to Yusuf**, who works in a bank's mortgage office, and they're saving for a wedding.
Her fear is mostly for **Yusuf's desk job**, which goes before her own.
Her answers lean on **family and faith**: marry small, live with parents, learn trades.
She wants **paid apprenticeships**, not handouts, and is stubborn about keeping her own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes would be hit with no time.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships for adults** so people can learn a trade.
